clinician.trajectory_summary: A 54-year-old farmer with a 46 pack-year smoking history presented with a 10-month history of productive cough with yellowish sputum and moderate hemoptysis, accompanied by fever and altered general condition. On admission, he was found to be hypoxic (89% on room air), tachypneic (24 cycles/min), with dullness to percussion over the entire left hemithorax and bilateral axillary adenopathies. Chest X-ray revealed a hydro-pneumothorax appearance. Chest CT imaging demonstrated a left lung abscess communicating with lobar bronchi, left pyopneumothorax, and right peribronchovascular micronodules with infectious appearance. Pleural puncture yielded chocolate-colored purulent fluid. Direct microscopic examination revealed numerous filamentous gram-positive bacilli initially suggestive of actinomyces. TB testing (BK and GeneXpert MTB/RIF) in pleural fluid and sputum was negative. Laboratory workup showed significant inflammatory response (CRP 180 mg/L), microcytic hypochromic anemia (8.1 g/dL), hyperleukocytosis (16,000/mm³ with neutrophil predominance), hyperglycemia (2.1 g/L), and negative HIV serology. The diagnosis of pulmonary nocardiosis was confirmed by bacteriological study of the pleural fluid through direct examination and positive culture identifying Nocardia species.

Physical examination findings consistent with left-sided pleural involvement and systemic disease

Pleural fluid direct examination revealed filamentous gram-positive bacilli initially suggestive of actinomyces
Tuberculosis was excluded as the causative agent
Significant systemic inflammatory response and laboratory abnormalities consistent with severe infection
Pleural fluid bacteriological study confirmed Nocardia species, establishing the diagnosis of pulmonary nocardiosis

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: BK and GeneXpert MTB/RIF testing in both pleural fluid and sputum were negative (E003), effectively ruling out TB despite the clinical presentation being compatible with TB

HIV serology was negative (E004), ruling out HIV as a contributing immunosuppressive factor
